How do different laser types work?
There are two main types of laser (optical and IR):
Optical laser (optic): Optical lasers include CO2, Nd:YAG, erbium, neodymium and titanium. These lasers emit light through stimulated fluorescence, which refers to the emission of photons of lower energy than the absorbed photons by a high-energy atom. Fluorescence lasers are used for measuring up to 100 meters; they are the most affordable and easiest to use.
Infrared laser (IR): Infrared lasers include Nd:YAG, CO2, diode, Ti:Sapphire, diode, diode, and CO2 laser. These lasers emit light through an electromagnetic interaction, which refers to the emission of photons of higher energy than the absorbed photons by an electrically charged atom. IR lasers emit light with less than 40 nm wavelength for measuring up to 1,000 meters. Infrared lasers are the most expensive and more complex option. Depending on project needs, both light sources are excellent for measuring both up to 300 meters (with optical lasers) and up to 1,000 to 2,500 meters (with infrared lasers).
How do laser measuring tools work?
Each laser distance meter contains a laser that emits a light beam, which is reflected back when it hits a surface. The sensor in the laser distance meter measures the speed of the reflected light and calculates the distance by multiplying it by the time it took to get to the surface. Laser distance meters allow you to choose from one of two operating modes:
"Manual mode": Measures the distance manually by holding the laser distance meter near the point of interest and pressing a button. This method requires training and practice to get accurate readings.
"Automatic mode": Measures distances automatically by scanning the area with the laser distance meter and then highlighting the measurement on the screen. This method is less labor-intensive, but the technology has certain limitations and requires training and practice to use effectively.
What is the purpose of laser distance meters?
Laser distance meters are used for measuring both straight-line and curved distances, including:
In construction: Measuring materials
In carpentry: Measuring wood planks
In surveying: Measuring distances between points
In welding: Measuring the gap between two pieces of metal
